overview.prompt: A client is being evaluated for Ménière’s disease. Which symptoms make up its characteristic pattern? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sensorineural hearing loss
Recurrent spontaneous vertigo
Aural fullness or pressure
Brief vertigo on rolling in bed
Loss of consciousness in spells

overview.rationale: The characteristic pattern is recurrent spontaneous vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness/pressure. Brief position-triggered vertigo suggests a different pattern such as BPPV, and drop attacks classically occur without loss of consciousness.

overview.prompt: A client asks what “endolymphatic hydrops” means. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Calcium crystals loose in the semicircular canals
Infection of the middle ear behind the eardrum
Excess inner-ear fluid distending the labyrinth
A benign tumor pressing on the vestibular nerve

overview.rationale: Endolymphatic hydrops is excess/distension of endolymph within the membranous labyrinth. Middle-ear infection, loose crystals (BPPV), and vestibular schwannoma are different conditions.

overview.prompt: A client with Ménière’s disease asks, “What caused this?” Which response is most accurate?

options.text: “It is caused by a middle-ear infection.”
“It is caused by eating too much salt.”
“The cause isn’t fully understood yet.”
“It is passed directly from a parent.”

overview.rationale: The underlying cause remains incompletely understood and may involve genetic, immune, and environmental factors. Salt, infection, or inheritance alone are not established universal causes.

manifestations.prompt: A client describes episodes of spinning vertigo with nausea and ear fullness. Which episode pattern fits definite Ménière’s disease?

options.text: Lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, then easing
Lasting seconds, set off by head turns
Lasting under a minute after standing
Continuous for days without easing

manifestations.rationale: Definite Ménière’s attacks last 20 minutes to 12 hours; probable disease can include episodes up to 24 hours. Seconds-long or continuous multiday vertigo suggests other causes.

manifestations.prompt: Which audiogram pattern does the nurse expect early in Ménière’s disease?

options.text: Sudden complete loss in both ears at onset
Fluctuating low- to mid-frequency loss in one ear
Stable high-frequency loss affecting both ears
Conductive loss from fluid behind the eardrum

manifestations.rationale: Early hearing loss is often low- to mid-frequency and fluctuating, usually in one ear initially. The other patterns are not the typical early presentation.

manifestations.prompt: A client with Ménière’s disease suddenly falls to the floor without warning but remains fully conscious. How should the nurse describe this?

options.text: Orthostatic faint
Syncopal episode
Generalized seizure
Tumarkin drop attack

manifestations.rationale: Tumarkin drop attacks are abrupt vestibular falls, classically without loss of consciousness, and may occur without warning. Loss of consciousness would suggest syncope or seizure.

manifestations.prompt: A client with known Ménière’s disease reports a sudden major drop in hearing in one ear since this morning. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait for the routine audiology visit
Reassure that this is expected progression
Arrange an urgent medical assessment
Advise a lower-sodium diet for now

manifestations.rationale: A new sudden major hearing change needs urgent assessment, even in a person with known Ménière’s disease. Assuming expected progression or waiting delays care.

risk.prompt: A nurse is reviewing risk patterns for Ménière’s disease. When is onset most common?

options.text: In early childhood
During adolescence
In very late life
In middle adulthood

risk.rationale: Onset is most common in middle adulthood, often ages 40–60, though it can occur outside this range. Childhood, adolescent, or only very late onset are not the typical pattern.

risk.prompt: A client’s sibling asks how to prevent getting Ménière’s disease. Which response is accurate?

options.text: “Annual MRI scans will prevent it from starting.”
“Giving up caffeine will stop it developing.”
“There’s no established way to prevent all cases.”
“A strict no-sugar diet will prevent it.”

risk.rationale: There is no established way to prevent all Ménière’s disease because its cause is uncertain. Early assessment of recurrent vertigo with ear symptoms is encouraged.

diagnostics.prompt: Which finding is part of the criteria for a definite Ménière’s diagnosis?

options.text: A positive blood test specific for Ménière’s disease
A single prolonged vertigo episode lasting days
At least 2 spontaneous attacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours
Brief vertigo triggered by rolling over in bed

diagnostics.rationale: Definite disease requires at least 2 spontaneous vertigo episodes lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, documented low- to mid-frequency SNHL, and fluctuating aural symptoms. No blood test confirms it.

diagnostics.prompt: A client reports brief spinning episodes only when turning over in bed, with no hearing changes. What does this pattern suggest?

options.text: A different disorder such as BPPV
Early definite Ménière’s disease
Early probable Ménière’s disease
A Tumarkin drop attack pattern

diagnostics.rationale: Brief position-triggered episodes suggest a different pattern such as BPPV. Ménière’s episodes are spontaneous and last 20 minutes or longer with aural symptoms.

diagnostics.prompt: A client with asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss is scheduled for an MRI. The client asks why. What is the best explanation?

options.text: To measure the fluid pressure inside the inner ear
To confirm Ménière’s disease in typical cases
To check for loose calcium crystals in the ear canals
To evaluate alternatives such as vestibular schwannoma

diagnostics.rationale: MRI may be offered for asymmetric sensorineural loss to evaluate alternatives such as vestibular schwannoma; it is not a compulsory confirmatory scan for every typical case.

medical.prompt: A client asks about trying a Meniett positive-pressure device for persistent vertigo. What does the nurse know about current AAO-HNS guidance?

options.text: It is the standard next treatment for vertigo
It is recommended for most new diagnoses
It is required before medications are tried
It is advised against for this condition

medical.rationale: AAO-HNS recommends against prescribing positive-pressure therapy for Ménière’s disease; it is not the routine next treatment.

medical.prompt: A client with refractory vertigo asks about labyrinthectomy. For whom is this procedure generally reserved?

options.text: Clients with normal hearing in the affected ear
Clients with a poor or nonfunctional hearing ear
Clients with a first episode of vertigo
Clients who have not yet tried treatment

medical.rationale: Labyrinthectomy sacrifices residual hearing and is generally reserved for a poorly/nonfunctional hearing ear after less definitive treatment. It is not used for ears with normal hearing, first episodes, or untreated disease.

medical.prompt: Between attacks, which maintenance option may be offered to selected clients with Ménière’s disease?

options.text: Continuous daily meclizine
Positive-pressure therapy
Daily long-term diazepam
Diuretics and/or betahistine

medical.rationale: Diuretics and/or betahistine may be offered for maintenance in selected patients. Benzodiazepines and meclizine are short-course rescue drugs, and positive pressure is not recommended.

medications.prompt: A client is starting HCTZ for Ménière’s maintenance and asks when to take it. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Take it in the late evening
Take it as an attack begins
Take it early in the day
Take it just before bed

medications.rationale: HCTZ is generally given early in the day to limit nocturia. Evening or bedtime doses increase night urination, and it is maintenance therapy, not immediate rescue.

medications.prompt: A client takes HCTZ/triamterene and plans to start a potassium salt substitute. What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: Use it to replace potassium lost from HCTZ
Add potassium pills for extra protection
Avoid it due to the risk of hyperkalemia
Eat extra bananas to boost potassium

medications.rationale: Triamterene spares potassium, so HCTZ/triamterene can cause hyperkalemia. Do not self-start potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes. Potassium advice depends on renal function, laboratory results, and the prescribed plan; uncommon significant hypokalemia requires clinician-directed management rather than routine replacement.

medications.prompt: A client taking HCTZ alone reports muscle cramps and weakness. Which electrolyte change should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Hypokalemia
Hypernatremia
Hyperkalemia
Hypercalcemia

medications.rationale: HCTZ alone can cause hypokalemia, which may present with weakness and cramps. Hyperkalemia is a risk with potassium-sparing combinations.

medications.prompt: A client received diazepam for severe vertigo and is now drowsy. A student suggests giving flumazenil. What should the nurse know?

options.text: Flumazenil may be given freely with little risk
Flumazenil may take the place of airway support
Flumazenil may precipitate seizures or withdrawal
Flumazenil may be given after each dose routinely

medications.rationale: Flumazenil is for selected monitored situations, and it can precipitate seizures/withdrawal. Airway and breathing support come first.

medications.prompt: A client asks if she should take meclizine every day to prevent attacks. What is the best response?

options.text: “Use only the limited course prescribed.”
“Double the dose whenever you feel dizzy.”
“Take it each day on a long-term basis.”
“Take it with alcohol to boost its effect.”

medications.rationale: Meclizine is used as the prescribed limited course, not automatic continuous daily suppression. Alcohol increases impairment.

nonpharmacological.prompt: A client feels a vertigo spell beginning while at the grocery store. What should the nurse have taught?

options.text: Walk quickly to the car and drive straight home
Keep shopping and focus on a fixed object
Sit or lie down safely and minimize head movement
Climb the stairs to reach a quieter area

nonpharmacological.rationale: At onset, sit or lie down in a safe place, obtain assistance, and minimize head movement. Driving, walking alone, or stairs during vertigo are unsafe.

nonpharmacological.prompt: A client is having an acute severe spinning attack, and a family member asks about vestibular rehabilitation exercises now. What is the best response?

options.text: “It replaces the medicines during an episode.”
“Do the hardest exercises during each spell.”
“It’s for chronic imbalance, not this spell.”
“Start the exercises now to stop the spinning.”

nonpharmacological.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation is for chronic imbalance and is not the treatment for an acute spinning attack; provocative exercises are avoided during a severe spell.

adverse-effects.prompt: After receiving diazepam and promethazine, a client is difficult to arouse with slow, shallow breathing. What is the nurse’s priority?

options.text: Treat as an emergency and support the airway
Let the client sleep off the vertigo spell
Recheck vital signs at the next routine check
Give another dose to keep them comfortable

adverse-effects.rationale: Difficult arousal or slow/shallow breathing is an emergency; it should not be assumed to be ordinary fatigue after vertigo.

adverse-effects.prompt: An hour after promethazine, a client develops abnormal twisting of the neck and tongue. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Dystonia, an extrapyramidal effect
Hypokalemia caused by vomiting
Expected drowsiness from the drug
A new Ménière’s vertigo attack

adverse-effects.rationale: Watch for dystonia/abnormal eye, neck, or tongue movements and other EPS after promethazine, and follow urgent treatment protocols. These movements are not vertigo, sedation, or an electrolyte effect.

adverse-effects.prompt: A client takes HCTZ for Ménière’s disease. Which adverse effects should the nurse monitor for? Select all that apply.

options.text: Low uric acid levels
Low blood glucose levels
Low serum potassium
High potassium from HCTZ
Orthostatic hypotension

adverse-effects.rationale: HCTZ may cause dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, low sodium/potassium/magnesium, glucose elevation, or hyperuricemia. Hyperkalemia is a risk with potassium-sparing agents, not HCTZ alone, and HCTZ raises rather than lowers glucose and uric acid.

nutrition.prompt: A client with Ménière’s disease is asked to try a lower-sodium plan. How should the sodium goal be set?

options.text: Left unrestricted while taking a diuretic
As the lowest intake the client can manage
As an individualized target with the team
As one standard limit used for each client

nutrition.rationale: A commonly used individualized target is 1,500–2,000 mg sodium/day, not a universal requirement. Extremely low or unlimited intake is not advised, especially with diuretics.

nutrition.prompt: A client eats very little salt on weekdays but large salty restaurant meals on weekends. What should the nurse advise?

options.text: Cut sugar instead of limiting salt
Avoid large swings in salt intake
Save the weekly salt for one day
Drink large volumes to flush salt

nutrition.rationale: Avoid large swings in salt intake and spread intake through the day; forcing water or cutting all sugar is not established.

assessment.prompt: A client with known Ménière’s disease has vertigo plus new slurred speech and double vision. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Arrange urgent evaluation for stroke
Treat as a typical Ménière’s attack
Give meclizine and reassess later
Perform a Romberg test first

assessment.rationale: A known Ménière’s diagnosis does not rule out stroke or another acute disorder; dysarthria and diplopia require urgent evaluation.

assessment.prompt: A client is vomiting and cannot sit up without severe spinning. When should the nurse perform a Romberg test?

options.text: Perform it now to confirm diagnosis
Defer it until the client is stable
Have the client stand unassisted
Test with eyes closed while walking

assessment.rationale: Assess balance only with guarding when safe and defer Romberg during severe instability; it is nonspecific.

diagnoses.prompt: A client has sudden drop attacks and takes meclizine. Which nursing diagnosis is best supported?

options.text: Excess fluid volume
Risk for falls/injury
Risk for bleeding
Impaired swallowing

diagnoses.rationale: Risk for falls/injury relates to episodic vertigo, drop attacks, chronic imbalance, or sedating medicines. The other diagnoses are not supported.

diagnoses.prompt: During an attack, a client is nauseated and vomiting. What is the nausea most directly related to?

options.text: Vestibular disturbance
Low blood glucose
High-sodium meals
Gastric ulcer disease

diagnoses.rationale: Nausea related to vestibular disturbance is the supported diagnosis when present; the other causes are not indicated.

priorities.prompt: A client with Ménière’s disease begins a severe vertigo attack while walking in the hallway. What is the nurse’s first action?

options.text: Give an oral antiemetic right away
Perform a bedside hearing test
Help the client sit or lie down safely
Walk the client back to the room now

priorities.rationale: First help the patient sit/lie safely and assess stability, injury, and neurological/hearing changes. Walking the client, giving oral medicine first, or testing hearing delays fall prevention.

priorities.prompt: A client says, “I always feel ear fullness before an attack, so I can keep driving.” Why should the nurse not rely on warning symptoms?

options.text: Warning signs may last several hours
Drop attacks may occur without warning
Fullness may mean an attack is unlikely
Fullness may reliably signal each attack

priorities.rationale: Do not rely on warning fullness/tinnitus, because drop attacks can occur without warning; individualized driving restrictions are discussed.

plan.prompt: Which goal best addresses safety and acute symptom control during an attack?

options.text: Walking unassisted throughout the attack
No further attacks after this one episode
Deep sedation until symptoms have stopped
No preventable falls, with safe transfers

plan.rationale: The goal is no preventable fall/injury, with nausea/vertigo settling enough for safe assisted transfers without excessive sedation. No treatment guarantees no future attacks.

plan.prompt: How should function and hearing goals be evaluated for a client with Ménière’s disease?

options.text: Assume that further attacks will not occur
Track attacks, ADLs, and how they communicate
Judge success by the latest audiogram alone
Promise that normal hearing will come back

plan.rationale: Evaluate attack pattern, falls, ADLs, and communication rather than promising cure or normal hearing. A single audiogram does not capture overall function.

interventions.prompt: A client with Ménière’s hearing loss is receiving discharge teaching. Which communication technique is best?

options.text: Talk quickly so that the session stays brief
Speak from behind to avoid startling the client
Shout so the client can hear the teaching well
Face the client, speak clearly, and reduce noise

interventions.rationale: Face the patient, speak clearly without shouting, reduce background noise, and confirm understanding. Shouting distorts speech and speaking from behind removes visual cues.

interventions.prompt: During a severe vertigo spell, which nursing intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Assist positioning; provide a quiet, dim room
Encourage walking alone to the bathroom now
Move the client quickly to a different room
Turn on the bright overhead lights for safety

interventions.rationale: Assist safe positioning, toileting/ADLs, fall precautions, an emesis container, and a quiet/dim environment as tolerated; avoid abrupt position changes.

education.prompt: A client with tinnitus asks about OTC pain relievers. Which medicine can worsen tinnitus at high doses?

options.text: Plain acetaminophen tablets
Topical lidocaine patches
Aspirin and other salicylates
Saline nasal spray as needed

education.rationale: Salicylates/aspirin and some other drugs can worsen tinnitus, especially at high doses; prescribed low-dose cardiac aspirin should not be stopped independently.

education.prompt: A client on HCTZ has had substantial vomiting for a day. What should the client be taught to do?

options.text: Contact the team for medicine and fluid advice
Double the HCTZ dose to clear extra fluid
Stop drinking fluids until the vomiting ends
Keep taking HCTZ as usual without changes

education.rationale: During substantial vomiting, contact the team for medication/fluid advice rather than continuing blindly or changing doses independently. Restricting fluids worsens dehydration.

evaluation.prompt: A client’s audiogram shows slight further loss despite good adherence. How should the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: Good adherence means hearing is protected
Treatment has failed and should be stopped
Some progression is possible with good care
The audiogram result is likely in error

evaluation.rationale: Normal hearing or prevention of all progression is not a required or guaranteed outcome; changes receive appropriate assessment.

evaluation.prompt: A client takes betahistine exactly as prescribed but still has frequent attacks. How should the nurse evaluate whether the medicine is working?

options.text: By the count of tablets taken each week
By how closely it is taken as ordered
By its real effect on symptom control
By the lack of side effects reported

evaluation.rationale: Evaluate each therapy’s benefit rather than inferring success solely from adherence. Pill counts or lack of side effects do not show that attacks are controlled.
